subject: physics_2
question_text: Derive the equation for couple acting on an electric dipole in uniform electric field.

mark_split.label: The two forces form a couple
τ = pE sin θ and vector form

verification.note: The 1+1+1+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. For this Physics-II paper the two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only, and the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers. Hand-checked: forces +qE and −qE give zero net force; torque = force × perpendicular distance = qE × 2a sin θ = pE sin θ; vector form τ = p × E, perpendicular to both p and E. The book writes the dipole moment as capital P (printed p.20); the standard lowercase p is used here. The book's question prints 'a electric dipole'; written as 'an electric dipole'.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: The dipole in the field
lines: Consider an electric dipole with charges +q
and −q separated by a distance 2a, placed
in a uniform electric field E with its axis
at an angle θ to the field.
Its dipole moment is p = q × 2a, directed
steps.margin_note: First mark. Name every symbol the result will use: q, 2a, E, θ and p.
steps.why: The final answer is written in p, E and θ, so all three must be defined at the start — p as charge times separation, θ as the angle between the dipole axis and the field.
common_mistakes: Writing p = q × a. The separation of the charges is 2a, so p = q × 2a.
Taking θ from the perpendicular instead of from the field direction.

recall.must_convey: That a dipole of moment p = q × 2a sits in a uniform field E at angle θ.
accept: charges plus q and minus q separated by 2a
axis at angle theta to the field

steps.memory_tip: Define before you derive: q, 2a, E, θ — and p = q × 2a from them.

steps.label: The figure
steps.margin_note: The dipole at angle θ to the field, the force +qE on +q along E, −qE on −q opposite to E, and the dashed perpendicular distance 2a sin θ between the two lines of action.
steps.why: The mark-carrying length 2a sin θ can only be SEEN — it is the perpendicular distance between the two parallel force lines, and the dashed construction line is what makes the torque formula readable.
common_mistakes: Drawing both forces in the same direction. They are equal and OPPOSITE — that is why the net force is zero.
Labelling the dashed distance 2a. The separation along the axis is 2a; the distance between the force lines is 2a sin θ.

recall.must_convey: That the figure shows the tilted dipole in the uniform field with forces +qE and −qE and the perpendicular distance 2a sin θ.
accept: draw the dipole at angle theta with the two forces
mark 2a sin theta between the force lines
reject: torque equals force into perpendicular distance

steps.memory_tip: Two equal opposite arrows on a tilted rod — then drop the dashed perpendicular between them.

steps.label: The two forces form a couple
lines: The field exerts a force qE on +q along E,
and a force qE on −q opposite to E. The net
force on the dipole is zero, but the two
forces act at different points, so they
form a couple and rotate the dipole.
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Two claims: net force zero, AND the two forces form a couple.
steps.why: Equal and opposite forces cancel as a push but not as a turn — acting at different points they form a couple, which is why the dipole rotates instead of moving away.
common_mistakes: Saying the dipole moves in the field. In a UNIFORM field the net force is zero — it only rotates.
Writing the forces as qE and −q. The force on each charge has magnitude qE.

recall.must_convey: That the forces qE and qE are equal and opposite at different points, so the net force is zero and a couple acts.

steps.memory_tip: Zero push, pure turn — equal opposite forces at two points are a couple.

steps.label: Torque of the couple
lines: Torque of a couple = one force ×
forces. From the figure this distance is
steps.margin_note: Third mark. The perpendicular distance is 2a sin θ, read off the figure.
steps.why: A couple's torque is one force times the perpendicular distance between the two lines of action. The geometry of the tilted dipole makes that distance 2a sin θ — the sine is where θ enters the result.
common_mistakes: Using 2a cos θ. The perpendicular distance between the force lines involves sin θ.
Multiplying by BOTH forces. A couple's torque uses ONE force times the perpendicular distance.

recall.must_convey: That the torque is one force qE times the perpendicular distance 2a sin θ.

steps.memory_tip: One force, one perpendicular distance — qE times 2a sin θ.

steps.label: τ = pE sin θ
steps.mark_note: τ = pE sin θ · τ = p × E

lines.text: τ = (q × 2a) E sin θ = pE sin θ

lines: In vector form τ = p × E. The direction of
τ is perpendicular to both p and E.

lines.text: τ = pE sin θ · τ = p × E

steps.margin_note: Last mark. Substitute p = q × 2a, then give the vector form with its direction.
steps.why: Grouping q × 2a into p turns the geometry into the standard result τ = pE sin θ, and the cross product p × E packs both the magnitude and the perpendicular direction into one line.
common_mistakes: Writing τ = pE cos θ. Torque is maximum when the dipole is PERPENDICULAR to the field (θ = 90°), so it must be sin θ.
Writing τ = E × p. The order matters in a cross product: τ = p × E.

recall.must_convey: That τ = pE sin θ, and in vector form τ = p × E, perpendicular to both.
accept: perpendicular to both p and E

steps.memory_tip: Check the limits: θ = 0 gives no torque, θ = 90° gives the maximum pE — only sin θ does both.

insider_note: The figure earns its keep at the third mark — 2a sin θ must be visible as the dashed distance between the two force lines, not pulled from memory.
